title: Merge Sort & Divide-and-Conquer Sorting
summary: The divide-and-conquer sort that guarantees O(n log n) in every case and preserves the order of equal keys, at the cost of O(n) auxiliary memory.

slides.markdown:
Merge sort's whole idea fits in one sentence: **split the array in half, sort each half, merge the two sorted halves.** The splitting bottoms out at arrays of size one — trivially sorted — and the real work happens on the way back up, in the merge.

That merge step is the reason merge sort is worth knowing beyond "another O(n log n) sort": it's the only classic comparison sort that guarantees O(n log n) in the **worst case**, guarantees **stability**, and needs no random access — which makes it the natural sort for linked lists and for data too large to fit in memory.

The price for all of that is O(n) extra space. Quicksort trades the stability and worst-case guarantee away to sort in place; that trade-off is the subject of the next topic.

slides.subTitle: Combining two sorted halves in linear time
slides.markdown:
Given two already-sorted arrays, you can produce one sorted array of both in a single pass, without ever going back to re-examine an element.

Keep a pointer into each half and a pointer into the output. At every step, compare the two elements the half-pointers are looking at, copy the smaller one to the output, and advance that half's pointer. When one half runs out, copy the rest of the other half over — it's already sorted, so no more comparisons are needed.

Every element is copied exactly once, and every comparison advances a pointer, so the merge of two halves totalling n elements costs **O(n)** — not O(n log n), just the merge itself. The `log n` comes from how many times you have to merge (next slide), not from the merge step.

slides.sectionTitle: Merge sort — recursive divide plus merge
slides.markdown:
The recursive shape is the same in every language: split, recurse on each half, merge.

```python
def merge_sort(arr):
    if len(arr) <= 1:
        return arr
    mid = len(arr) // 2
    left = merge_sort(arr[:mid])
    right = merge_sort(arr[mid:])
    return merge(left, right)

def merge(left, right):
    result = []
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:   # <= keeps equal keys stable
            result.append(left[i]); i += 1
        else:
            result.append(right[j]); j += 1
    result.extend(left[i:])
    result.extend(right[j:])
    return result
```

The `<=` in the comparison is not cosmetic — it's what makes the sort stable (slide 6). Flip it to `<` and equal keys can swap order.

slides.subTitle: log n levels, each doing O(n) work
slides.markdown:
Draw the recursion as a tree: the root is the full array, each node splits into two children of half the size, down to leaves of size 1. Splitting in half every time means the tree has **⌈log₂ n⌉ levels**.

Now look at one level instead of one node. At depth k there are 2^k subarrays, each of size n / 2^k, and merging pairs at that level touches every element exactly once — so **each full level costs O(n)** in total merge work, regardless of depth.

Multiply: `O(n)` work per level times `O(log n)` levels gives **O(n log n)** total. This level-by-level accounting is the cleanest way to derive the bound, and it's the same argument you'll reuse for any balanced divide-and-conquer recurrence, `T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)`.

slides.sectionTitle: Why merge sort is O(n log n) even in the worst case
slides.markdown:
Merge sort's split point never depends on the data — it's always the midpoint, no matter what values are in the array. That's the key difference from quicksort, whose split point depends on a chosen pivot and the data around it.

Because the split is data-independent, the recursion tree always has exactly `log₂ n` levels and each level always costs `O(n)`, whatever the input looks like: sorted, reverse-sorted, all duplicates, adversarially chosen — none of it changes the shape of the tree.

That's why merge sort's **best, average, and worst case are all Θ(n log n)**. There is no unlucky input. Interviewers ask this specifically to check whether you know that quicksort's O(n²) worst case comes from a *data-dependent* split, and merge sort's guarantee comes from *not having one*.

slides.sectionTitle: Stability: merge sort preserves the relative order of equal keys
slides.markdown:
A sort is **stable** if two elements with equal keys keep their original relative order after sorting. Merge sort is stable, and it's stable *because of one line*: in the merge step, when `left[i]` and `right[j]` are equal, you take from `left` first (the `<=` comparison in the code slide).

Since `left` always came from an earlier position in the original array than `right`, always breaking ties toward `left` means an element that started earlier never gets pulled behind an equal one that started later.

Stability matters whenever you sort by one key after already sorting by another — sort a table of orders by customer name, and a stable sort keeps each customer's orders in their original date order for free. Quicksort and heapsort, in their standard forms, don't offer this guarantee.

slides.sectionTitle: Merge sort on linked lists: no random access needed
slides.markdown:
Quicksort's partitioning wants to jump around and swap elements at arbitrary indices — expensive on a linked list, where reaching index k means walking k pointers. Merge sort never does that: splitting just needs to find the middle node, and merging just needs to follow `next` pointers forward, never backward.

Finding the middle is itself O(n) per call via the classic **slow/fast pointer** technique (fast moves two nodes for every one the slow pointer moves; when fast hits the end, slow is at the middle), but it costs no more than the merge step already does, so the overall O(n log n) is unaffected.

This is why merge sort is the textbook answer to "sort a linked list in O(n log n) time and O(1) *extra* space" — the merge itself relinks existing nodes instead of allocating a new array, so the O(n) auxiliary cost from the array version disappears.

slides.sectionTitle: External sorting: merging chunks too large to fit in memory
slides.markdown:
Merge sort's real-world job is sorting data that doesn't fit in RAM — server logs, a multi-terabyte table dump. This is **external sorting**, and it's merge sort's merge step scaled up to disk.

The pattern: read as much data as fits in memory, sort that chunk in RAM (with any in-memory sort), write it back to disk as a sorted **run**. Repeat until the whole file is a sequence of sorted runs. Then merge the runs — often many at once with a **k-way merge** using a heap to pick the smallest of k current run-heads — writing the result back out, until one fully sorted file remains.

The reason this is merge sort and not, say, external quicksort: merging sorted runs only ever reads each one sequentially, forward, which is exactly what spinning disks and even SSDs are fast at. Quicksort's random-access partitioning would thrash the disk.

Both orderings do the same merges — they just build the tree in opposite directions.

| | Top-down | Bottom-up |
|---|---|---|
| Direction | Recurse down to size-1, merge on the way back up | Start by merging size-1 pairs, then size-2, then size-4… |
| Call stack | O(log n) recursion depth | None — a simple loop |
| Code shape | Shorter, matches the "divide then conquer" mental model | An outer loop over merge width, doubling each pass |
| Where it's used | Most textbook and interview implementations | Preferred when recursion depth or call overhead is a concern |

Bottom-up is worth knowing because it's the version that generalizes directly to external sorting (previous slide): "merge width" there is just "how many runs I combine per pass," and there's no recursion to manage across disk I/O boundaries.

slides.sectionTitle: Merging in place naively and overwriting data you haven't read yet
slides.markdown:
A tempting "optimization": skip the auxiliary array and merge the two halves directly inside the original array, writing results over the same memory you're reading from.

The bug: the output pointer and the read pointers walk the *same* region, and the output can catch up to and overwrite an element the read side hasn't consumed yet. Once that happens the merge silently produces wrong output — no crash, no exception, just a subtly unsorted result that only shows up on certain input patterns.

True in-place merging (O(1) extra space) is possible but requires a genuinely different algorithm — block-based rotations, not a naive index-shuffle — and it's rarely worth the complexity. If you're asked for in-place merge sort in an interview, say this out loud: it's a known hard variant, not a five-minute tweak to the standard merge.

slides.sectionTitle: Forgetting merge sort's O(n) auxiliary space when the problem demands O(1) extra
slides.markdown:
"Sort this array in O(n log n) time" and "sort this array in O(n log n) time and O(1) extra space" are different questions, and merge sort only answers the first one. The standard array implementation allocates a new array for every merge — Θ(n) auxiliary space at the top level (the temporary buffers at each level are typically reused, but the peak is still Θ(n)).

If a problem statement says "in place" or gives you a tight memory budget, that's usually a signal toward **heapsort** (true O(1) extra, same O(n log n) worst case) or **quicksort** (O(log n) expected recursion stack, in-place partitioning) — see the next topic for that trade-off.

The fix in an interview isn't to force merge sort in place; it's to recognize the constraint and switch algorithms, and say why.
